The original English version remains the authoritative edition. Disputes arising under the license are to be mediated according to the rules of the World Intellectual Property Organization. This publication is part of the WHO guideline on digital interventions for strengthening health systems. It is made publicly available to ensure transparency and provide information, as required by WHO's guideline development handbook. The suggested citation for this work is: WHO guideline: recommendations on digital interventions for health system strengthening. Evidence on Birth and Death Notification via Mobile Devices: 1. Effectiveness of Death Notification: No evidence was identified regarding the effectiveness of death notification via mobile devices. 2. Certainty of Evidence: The certainty of evidence for outcomes such as coverage and timeliness of birth notification, as well as newborn or child healthcare services, was assessed as very low. No studies reported on resource use or unintended consequences. 3. Acceptability to Health Workers: Health workers generally find mobile phone use for birth and death notification acceptable and supportive of their responsibilities. Some report increased proactivity in identifying and reporting pregnancies due to phone reminders, as well as enhanced trust and respect within their communities. Others note that electronic reporting saves time compared to in-person reporting. 4. Acceptability to Clients: Sociocultural norms, such as the acknowledgment of stillbirths or maternal deaths, and financial barriers may hinder timely notification. Families may not perceive benefits in birth or death notification, necessitating demand-generation activities alongside mobile notification introduction. 5. Feasibility: Challenges include network connectivity, access to electricity, system integration, device usability, and data confidentiality. Geographic barriers and transportation issues may delay notifications. Some studies suggest that mobile devices can reduce these challenges by facilitating on-site birth certification and reducing trips to distant registration centers. Adequate local staffing and rigorous training are critical for success. Gender, Equity, and Human Rights Considerations: While mobile notification systems aim to reach under-registered populations, inequities in implementation arise due to infrastructure limitations, demographic factors (e.g., age, gender, literacy, poverty), and selective donor funding priorities. Health workers in rural areas may benefit from overcoming geographic barriers but face challenges such as poor network coverage, limited training, and fewer resources. Resource Requirements for Implementation: 1. Start-Up Costs: These include user-centered design processes, community outreach, and initial training. Costs vary depending on the scope of activities, such as adapting training curricula and raising awareness through campaigns. 2. Ongoing Costs: These include refresher training, system maintenance, and communication expenses (e.g., SMS, data transmission). Hardware and software maintenance, including licensing and upgrades, are also required. 3. Integration with Registration Systems: This involves adapting content and technology to link notifications with birth and death registration systems, ensuring data security, and conducting user testing to optimize the intervention. Additional Considerations: Strong health and civil registration infrastructure, political will, and government support are essential for successful implementation. Legal frameworks may need modification to accommodate mobile notification systems and allow new types of health workers to issue certificates. Continuous monitoring and feedback mechanisms are critical to ensure data quality and timeliness.
